title: Tamsin and the Harvest
premise: Rosalind Eriksen, a nonbinary urban explorer and insomniac, has spent seven years documenting the unmapped tunnels beneath the drowned quarry town of Harrow's Bend, rationalizing every sound as settling earth or water. When their new sleep-recording rig captures a second voice answering questions Rosalind never asked aloud — in Rosalind's own voice — they discover the tunnels were dug to contain something the town's founders invited in, and that seven years of listening has been an invitation of its own. Trapped underground after a collapse seals the entrance, Rosalind must survive until sunrise alongside the last descendant of the founding families, a feral girl named Tamsin who was raised as the thing's keeper, while learning that the entity wears the voices of everyone it has taken. In the end, Rosalind refuses the bargain offered — to become the next keeper and walk free — and instead helps Tamsin unmake the invitation at dawn, escaping changed: no longer able to tell which voice inside them is truly theirs.
about_author: Ulyana Whitlock is the pen name of a former municipal surveyor who spent a decade mapping infrastructure beneath aging industrial towns before turning to fiction. Their work explores what people owe the places that raised them, and what those places take in return.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Establishes Rosalind's routine: mapping Harrow's Bend's storm drains by night, cataloging sounds they refuse to name. A tunnel appears on their hand-drawn map that matches nothing in any archive. Emotional beat: controlled denial, the comfort of systems and checklists over dread.

chapters.title: Seven Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Flashback interwoven with present: how Rosalind found the first wrong noise at twenty-three and built a taxonomy of rational causes. Their sister stops returning calls; Rosalind realizes the obsession cost them everyone. Beat: loneliness disguised as dedication.

chapters.title: What the Recorder Heard
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Reviewing sleep audio, Rosalind finds a second voice answering questions in the dark — questions asked in Rosalind's own voice. The answers are accurate about things only Rosalind knows. Beat: the floor drops out; denial becomes impossible.

chapters.title: Tamsin in the Drainage Cut
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Investigating the unmapped tunnel, Rosalind encounters Tamsin, a barefoot teenage girl who moves through the dark like she owns it and warns them off with words that are half threat, half liturgy. Beat: wary fascination; the first crack in isolation.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. In the county archive, Rosalind finds the Eriksen family name among Harrow's Bend founders — and a ledger page recording 'the arrangement,' renewed each generation by a named keeper. Beat: horror reframed as inheritance; Rosalind is not a visitor here.

chapters.title: Questions I Never Asked
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The second voice begins appearing while Rosalind is awake, faintly, from vents and pipe junctions, answering thoughts before they're spoken. Rosalind tests it with lies and it corrects them gently. Beat: paranoia curdling into terrible intimacy.

chapters.title: Keeper's Daughter
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin (first shift). Inside the tunnels, Tamsin performs her nightly rounds — feeding the thing, reciting the names — and resents the intruder who keeps coming closer. She reports to her dying grandmother that 'the listener' has been marked. Beat: duty as armor; Tamsin's fierce, frightened love for her grandmother.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Her grandmother confesses the truth: Tamsin was never born to be a child, but to be the next keeper, and the thing below has already chosen a replacement for Rosalind's role on the surface. Beat: betrayal braided with tenderness; Tamsin's loyalty begins to fracture.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Following the second voice to its source, Rosalind enters the founders' tunnel proper — brickwork older than the town, doors carved inward. Tamsin finds them there and, instead of driving them out, hesitates. Beat: two loners recognizing each other across enemy lines.

chapters.title: The Collapse
chapters.summary: POV alternating short sections. The thing below, impatient, brings down the tunnel mouth, sealing Rosalind and Tamsin inside together. Air is finite; sunrise is nine hours away. Beat: forced alliance; terror converted into cooperation.

chapters.title: Nine Hours
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Rosalind and Tamsin negotiate terms of truce by lamplight: Tamsin explains the rules (never answer it, never give your true name, never accept anything it offers). Rosalind admits they've broken all three for years. Beat: grim humor and growing trust.

chapters.title: It Knows My Mother's Voice
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The entity begins wearing voices — Rosalind's estranged sister, then Tamsin's grandmother, calling from side passages. Tamsin nearly follows hers; Rosalind physically holds her back. Beat: the test of loyalty vs. truth — love weaponized.

chapters.title: The Room of Names
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Tamsin leads Rosalind to the keeper's chamber: a wall of niches, each holding something belonging to a past keeper, including an Eriksen wedding ring. She reveals keepers don't die — they're kept. Beat: grief and rage; Tamsin decides her grandmother's death won't be honored by obedience.

chapters.title: An Offer, Politely Made
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The entity speaks directly, reasonably, in Rosalind's own voice: walk out now, live, and simply stop listening — or stay and learn everything. It shows Rosalind the exit, open, sunlit. Beat: temptation rendered as mercy; the cruelest chapter.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Tamsin tells the full origin: the founders didn't trap the thing, they summoned it to save the town from famine and paid in voices ever since. The invitation can be unmade — but only by someone it has marked, spoken aloud, at sunrise. Beat: hope with a price tag; Tamsin volunteers herself.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Rosalind rejects the offered exit, understanding at last that leaving means leaving Tamsin to pay alone — the same abandonment they've practiced their whole life. They choose to stay and be the one who speaks the unmaking. Beat: identity reclaimed; found family chosen over survival.

chapters.title: The Long Dark Before Dawn
chapters.summary: POV alternating. The final hours: the entity escalates, flooding passages, wearing every voice at once, offering each of them the other's life. Rosalind and Tamsin hold hands in the dark and trade true names — the one currency it cannot counterfeit between them. Beat: quiet intimacy at maximum danger.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. At first light they reach the heart chamber. Rosalind speaks the unmaking using their founder's blood-name; the entity fights back by becoming Rosalind's own recorded voice, pleading. Tamsin completes the rite when Rosalind falters. Beat: climax; sacrifice shared rather than borne alone.

chapters.title: Aftermath of a Voice
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. The tunnels go silent — truly silent — and the two dig out into morning. But Rosalind still hears a faint second voice sometimes, and can't tell if it's residue, memory, or themselves. Beat: hollowed-out relief; victory that doesn't feel clean.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Wasn't a Keeper
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Tamsin buries her grandmother above ground, in sunlight, breaking generations of practice. Rosalind offers her a place to stay — awkwardly, sincerely. Beat: mourning transformed into beginning; the found family takes shape.

chapters.title: Mapping What Remains
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Weeks later, Rosalind files the tunnel survey with the county under both their names — Eriksen and the girl's — making the hidden history official, un-ignorable. The second voice hasn't returned, or Rosalind has stopped distinguishing it. Beat: integration; living with ambiguity instead of denying it.

chapters.title: Tamsin and the Harvest
chapters.summary: POV dual, closing. On the anniversary, Rosalind and Tamsin return to the sealed tunnel mouth and leave offerings — not to the thing, but to everyone whose voices were taken. Tamsin asks what Rosalind will do with all the nights they used to spend listening. Rosalind says: spend them with someone. Beat: resolution — loyalty fulfilled, truth survived, identity shared.
